title: Advanced Model Binding Concepts in ASP.NET Core
description: Master binding source attributes (FromForm, FromBody, FromQuery, FromRoute, FromHeader) and collections binding.

data.text: ASP.NET Core's `model binding` automatically maps incoming HTTP request data to action method parameters. By default it searches form data, then route values, then query strings — in that order. But you can explicitly control where data is bound from using binding source attributes.

terms.definition: The automatic process of mapping HTTP request data to action method parameters.
An attribute like `[FromForm]` or `[FromQuery]` that tells model binding exactly which source to read from.
Key-value pairs sent in the body of an HTTP POST request.
Key-value pairs appended to a URL after the ? character.
Values extracted from the URL route pattern, such as {controller}, {action}, {id}.

data.caption: How ASP.NET Core model binding searches for values across different request sources.

data.text: ASP.NET Core provides five binding source attributes. Each one locks model binding to a single source, overriding the default search order.
Use `[FromForm]` when you want to explicitly read values from an HTML form submission. This is the default for MVC actions that accept POST requests, but adding it makes your intent clear.

data.title: Binding from a form
data.content: Read the Name field from the submitted form.

data.text: Use `[FromBody]` when the client sends JSON or XML in the request body. This is the standard approach for Web APIs.

data.title: Binding from JSON body
data.content: Deserialize the request body into a Product object.

data.text: Use `[FromQuery]` when you want to read filter or search parameters from the URL query string.

data.title: Binding from query string
data.content: Read page and pageSize from the query string.

data.text: Use `[FromRoute]` when you want to bind a parameter directly from a route segment. This is useful when the route parameter name does not match the action parameter name.

data.title: Binding from route
data.content: Bind the id parameter from the route segment.

data.text: Use `[FromHeader]` when you need to read custom headers sent by the client.

data.text: Model binding supports arrays and `List<T>`. When multiple form fields share the same name, ASP.NET Core automatically creates an array or `List<T>` from their values.

data.title: Practice: Build a Search API
data.description: Create a SearchController with actions that demonstrate each binding source attribute. Test each endpoint to confirm data is bound from the correct source.
steps: Create a SearchController with a GET action that uses [FromQuery] to accept a search term and page number.
Create a POST action that uses [FromForm] to accept a contact form (Name, Email, Message).
Create a POST action that uses [FromBody] to accept a JSON product object.
Create a GET action that uses [FromRoute] to accept an id from the URL.
Create a GET action that uses [FromHeader] to read a custom X-Correlation-Id header.
data.expectedOutcome: You understand when and how to use each binding source attribute to control where model binding reads data from.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Model binding searches form data, then route values, then query strings by default.
Use `[FromForm]`, `[FromBody]`, `[FromQuery]`, `[FromRoute]`, and `[FromHeader]` to control the binding source.
`[FromBody]` is the standard for Web APIs that consume JSON.
Collections bind from repeated field names (arrays) or indexed names (lists of complex types).
Binding source attributes make your code more explicit and prevent unexpected binding behavior.
data.takeaway: Binding source attributes give you precise control over where model binding reads data. Use them to make your action methods predictable and secure.
